title: Sweet Osmanthus: Ancient Osmanthus Trees You Can Visit
meta_description: A scent tree rarely protected by law, yet two of the three mapped here are National Natural Monuments, regrown from typhoon-felled originals in Gunma.
intro: Osmanthus fragrans is grown for one thing: for a few weeks each autumn, a mature tree's small flowers put out one of the strongest scents any hardy plant makes, apricot and ripe peach carried well past the tree itself. It rarely receives official protection of its own, which is what makes two of the three trees mapped here unusual: Gunma's Kezoji and Ora's Eimeiji examples both hold National Natural Monument status normally reserved for giant conifers and camphors. Both have also outlived their own trunks. Typhoons killed the original tree at each site, and what stands today grew back from the same root or stump, still carrying the designation. Caserta's tree, in the English Garden of the royal palace, is different again: it never fell, and its 6.5-metre girth is several stems bundled together rather than one trunk, which is how the species actually grows.
